entry.title: Institutional Response Tracker
entry.content:
From Courts to Checkpoints

The Anderson Localization analysis showed that captured judges create disorder in the judicial lattice. Cases that enter cannot propagate to a fair hearing.

But courts are not the only institutional checkpoint. Michigan has layered accountability structures: credentialing bodies, oversight commissions, authorizers, professional discipline departments, and law enforcement agencies. Each exists to catch what the others miss.

The question this page answers: When the same verified evidence is submitted to multiple institutional checkpoints simultaneously, which ones act and which ones don’t?

The answer reveals whether the accountability system functions or whether the disorder extends beyond the courts into the institutions designed to oversee them.

The Model

Every institutional checkpoint is a lattice site. Evidence arrives like an electron. Either the institution transmits it forward (investigation, action, referral) or it absorbs and traps it (closure, dismissal, non-response).

If every checkpoint absorbs, the system is fully localized. No accountability can propagate.

The measurement is simple:

InputWhat Was Submitted
SubjectBrian Roderick Banks: 9 criminal convictions (SID 2029469K), unauthorized use of “J.D.” credential, operation of two DPSCD-authorized charter schools
EvidenceICHAT criminal record, LARA corporate filings, MOECS credential audit, academic performance data (3% math proficiency), financial records ($4.9M revenue, 72.67% extraction to Purpose Group LLC), campaign finance data
FormatVerified public records, structured for independent verification
Sitedetroit.primals.eco

The same evidence package. Multiple institutions. Measure the output.

The Data

Checkpoint Response Table

This table is updated as responses arrive. Each row documents the institutional output for the same evidentiary input.

#InstitutionDepartmentFiledResponseDaysResult
1Michigan Dept. of EducationEducator Excellence20222022–Cleared with conditions
2Detroit Public Schools CDBoard of DirectorsJul 2025Jul 2025–Authorized second school
3State Bar of MichiganUPL Dept. (File 26-UP-51)Aug 2026Sep 30, 2026~30Administratively closed
4State Bar of MichiganUPL (2nd complaint)Sep 2026–PendingAwaiting response
5Baker CollegeHuman ResourcesOct 2026Oct 5, 2026<2Permanently severed
6Attorney Grievance CommissionProfessional discipline (x7)Sep-Oct 2026–PendingInvestigations pending
7Judicial Tenure CommissionJudicial conductSep 2026Sep 2026~5Investigations opened
8Central Michigan UniversityCharter authorizationPending––Notification staged
9MDE (Round 2)Credential re-examinationPending––Notification staged
10Detroit Inspector GeneralMunicipal oversightPending––Complaint staged

Key Observations

The only institution that acted in under 48 hours was a private employer with no regulatory obligation.

Baker College reviewed the same evidence that Michigan’s credentialing body, authorizing district, and professional bar department reviewed. Baker permanently severed ties. The regulatory bodies either cleared him, authorized him, or closed the complaint.

The UPL Department’s stated reason for closure: “Does not meet the standards set by the Unauthorized Practice of Law Committee to pursue this matter further.” The subject uses “J.D.” in professional communications, holds no bar admission in any jurisdiction, and operates a school named “School for Law and Public Service.”

The UPL Department’s stated alternative: “You may have other remedies available to you.”

The UPL complaint was the first of several submitted as the scope of the unauthorized credential use became clear through the investigation. Additional complaints remain pending and will be updated here as responses arrive.

The Asymmetry

Michigan’s system demands active defense from individuals:

  • A parent must file a motion and appear at a hearing to see their own children
  • A citizen must file an affirmative defense within 14 days to contest a personal protection order
  • A pro se litigant must meet the same procedural standards as a licensed attorney
  • A victim of assault must obtain and serve their own police report
  • A custody case requires the responding parent to affirmatively request the investigation the filing parent opted out of

But when a citizen uses the system’s own accountability tools:

  • A UPL complaint against a 9-time convicted felon using “J.D.” is closed as not meeting standards
  • An administrator certification for a habitual offender is granted with conditions
  • A second charter school is authorized for an operator whose first school ranks in the bottom 3% statewide
  • A police report filed at the scene of an assault requires the victim to drive to the precinct to retrieve it

The system enforces process against citizens aggressively. It declines to enforce against its own members passively.

This asymmetry is not incidental. It is the localization.

When the disorder in the lattice extends from the courts into the oversight bodies, the accountability signal has nowhere to propagate. Every checkpoint absorbs it. The individual is left with “other remedies available to you,” which means: the system has told you it will not help.

The Measurement Continues

This page is a living document. As institutional responses arrive, the table updates. Each response or non-response is a data point in the same experiment.

The question is not whether any single institution failed. Institutions make judgment calls. The question is whether the pattern of non-response across multiple independent checkpoints reveals structural localization rather than individual discretion.

When the same evidence produces action from a private college in 48 hours and produces closure from a state regulatory body in 30 days, the comparison is the finding. No editorial interpretation is required.

This is Anderson Localization measured in institutional responses rather than court assignments. The physics is the same: disorder prevents propagation. The measurement is how deep the disorder goes.

All submissions are documented. All responses are recorded as metadata. All claims are verifiable against public records. See Legal Protections for the First Amendment and fair comment framework.

Related: The pattern of institutions that ignore boundaries extends beyond Michigan oversight bodies. See Signal — Public Record of Automated Access for evidence of the same dynamic in corporate AI systems that access this investigation site: some check the rules and comply; others read the rules and scrape anyway.

entry.title: TCR 22-12 — The People Who Vouched
entry.content:
What Is TCR 22-12?

On August 4, 2023, State Superintendent Michael F. Rice granted Brian Banks a school administrator certificate despite 8 felony fraud convictions, subject to 7 conditions. The Michigan Department of Education’s own professional staff objected. The Attorney General’s office argued against granting it. Rice overruled his department.

Five people testified in Banks’s favor. Their testimony is public record. Their assessments can now be compared to Banks’s documented conduct in 2026.

The Department Objected

The Office of Educator Excellence — the people whose job is to evaluate whether someone should work in schools — raised formal objections to the ALJ’s recommendation. The AG’s office (Kathleen Halloran, Shelley McCormick) represented the department in opposing the certificate.

The professionals said no. The political appointee said yes.

The “Diagnoses” That Aren’t Diagnoses

Two professionals offered clinical-sounding assessments of Banks:

Terrence Shulman — Licensed Social Worker

  • Not a physician. Not a psychiatrist. Cannot diagnose.
  • Referred by State Bar of Michigan in 2011
  • 6 sessions in 2011, then 12 sessions in 2020-2021
  • Described Banks as “not dishonest as a matter of character”
  • Concurred with Leno’s PTSD finding — but a social worker cannot independently diagnose PTSD under the DSM-5
  • His specialty: “issues related to dishonesty” and “individuals who have had issues with various theft-related behaviors” — a niche practice focused on shoplifting and financial crime addiction

What he said: Banks “took ownership for all his actions and had paid off any debts he had owed.”

What happened: Banks told police “I am a lawyer” (2026). Banks has $14,500+ in unpaid PAC fines. Banks filed a retaliatory police report. The behavior didn’t stop — it evolved from checks and credit cards to claiming credentials he doesn’t have.

Michele Leno, Ph.D. — Licensed Psychologist

  • Psychologist (can diagnose), but assessment based on ~13 sessions over ~2 months (Dec 2020-Feb 2021)
  • Found Banks to be “a person of integrity”
  • Diagnosed PTSD from childhood adverse experiences
  • Said “no reason to believe criminal behavior will recur”
  • Found Banks “no longer in need of formal therapy”

What she said: Banks has integrity, won’t reoffend, and is “keenly focused on redemption.”

What happened: Three years later, Banks told police he is a lawyer (false), filed a retaliatory police report, denied a legal father’s representative access to his children’s school using false legal authority, and operates a $4.28M enterprise with a convicted drug offender and zero independent oversight.

What These Assessments Actually Are

Neither Shulman’s nor Leno’s evaluations are clinical diagnoses in the medical sense:

  • No psychiatric evaluation was conducted by an MD/DO
  • No standardized diagnostic testing referenced in the record
  • No longitudinal observation — Shulman had 18 total sessions over 10 years; Leno had 13 sessions over 2 months
  • The PTSD finding was based on self-reported childhood experiences, not clinical assessment with validated instruments
  • Both professionals’ practices are oriented toward rehabilitation advocacy, not forensic evaluation

These are character references with clinical language — verbal agreements between professionals outside the medical diagnostic field that Banks had changed. The language of diagnosis was used to give institutional weight to what is fundamentally an opinion.

Testimony vs. Reality

Who said itWhat they said (2023)What happened (2024-2026)
Shulman“Took ownership for all actions, paid off debts”Told police “I am a lawyer.” $14,500+ unpaid PAC fines.
Leno“Person of integrity. Criminal behavior will not recur.”False statement in government document. Retaliatory police report.
Wells-Stallworth“Position did not involve handling finances”Sole member of LLC receiving 72.67% of school revenue
Meihn“Integrity, honesty, transparency, compliance”False “No Related Parties” clause in Management Agreement
Vitti“Reflective, child-centric leader” 3% math proficiency. $4.28M extracted.
Shulman“I do not believe Mr. Banks suffers from any disorders”Diagnosed PTSD by Leno — contradictory findings
Leno“No longer in need of formal therapy”Banks’s conduct in 2026 suggests otherwise
Wells-Stallworth“Has gotten his life back on track”Co-residing with convicted drug offender managing entity finances
Meihn“Good people are few and far between”Holland concealed assets in bankruptcy to erase Banks as codebtor
Vitti“Skills, character, and integrity required”Banks denied father access to school, claimed to be lawyer

The 7 Conditions

The conditions imposed by Rice acknowledge the risk the enablers minimized:

  1. Remain free of financial convictions
  2. Provide this order to governing board
  3. Shall not handle cash
  4. Shall not be sole person to approve expenditures
  5. Submit compliance verification (current assignment)
  6. Submit compliance verification (future assignments)
  7. Every 6 months — written verification of #3 and #4, signed by board president

Who Signs the Verifications?

Nicole Wells-Stallworth — MacDowell Board President.

The same person who:

  • Hired Banks knowing his criminal history
  • Killed an MDE investigation in 2 hours 24 minutes
  • Is married into a political dynasty with a federal money laundering conviction
  • Whose stepdaughter sits on the DPSCD board that authorizes the charter

The compliance verification system relies on the enabler certifying the enabled.

The Condition #4 Evasion

Condition #4: Banks “shall not be the sole individual responsible for approval of any expenditure.”

Banks is sole member of Purpose Group LLC. Purpose Group receives $4,285,201 ( 72.67% ) of school revenue. All teachers and staff are employed by Purpose Group, not the school.

The entity structure routes school money through a private LLC where Banks IS the sole approval authority. Condition #4 is not violated at the school — because the money doesn’t stay at the school. It flows to Purpose Group, where no conditions apply.

The structure was designed to evade the condition.

Source Documents

  • TCR 22-12 Final Decision and Order (Aug 4, 2023) — 18 pages
  • TCR 22-12 Cover Letter — State Superintendent Rice
  • MDE FOIA Response (Sep 25, 2026)
  • MDE Supplemental Records (Sep 30, 2026 — unsolicited)

All documents received directly from Michigan Department of Education FOIA Coordinator David Head.

Verify

  • Contact MOAHR for full hearing transcript and exhibits
  • MDE: MDE-Professional-Practice@Michigan.gov
  • David Head, FOIA Coordinator: 517-855-1139

All sources: TCR 22-12 Final Decision (public record via MDE FOIA), hearing testimony as quoted in the decision.

entry.title: The Credential Gap — MacDowell Staff Qualification Audit
entry.content:
The Michigan Online Educator Certification System (MOECS) is the public database where anyone can verify whether a Michigan educator holds a valid teaching certificate, administrator certification, or permit — and which grade levels and subjects each endorsement covers. 📄 Documented

On September 26, 2026, every name listed on MacDowell Preparatory Academy’s public staff roster (macdowellprep.com/about/) was searched in MOECS. The audit found that only 2 of 14 instructional staff members are properly credentialed and correctly placed for their teaching assignment. 📄 Documented

Staff Roster Results 📄 Documented

Administration — 4 positions ($603,000/year combined)

RoleMOECS StatusIndicator
Superintendent/CAO (Brian Banks)Convicted felon (ICHAT SID 2029469K). School Administrator certificate only — no teaching credential.❌
Dean of Scholars + Culture (Cameron Coleman)Standard teaching certificate expired 6/30/2026. No administrator certification for Dean role.⏳
Dean of Academics (Kellie M Stevens)Standard teaching certificate (K-5/K-8 elementary). No administrator certification for Dean role.⚠️
Dean of Operations + 8th Grade Teacher (Chalcee Norwood)Not found in MOECS public search — 91 “Norwood” results searched, no match for “Chalcee”. Zero credentials discoverable.❌

Instructional Staff

RoleMOECS StatusIndicator
Kindergarten (Rachel Webb)Holds Secondary English/Journalism 6-12 certification. Zero elementary endorsement. Teaching kindergarten with a high school certificate.⚠️
Kindergarten (Lakeisha Bates)“No matches found” in MOECS. Zero credentials.❌
3rd Grade (Alana Hubbell)Daily Substitute Permit issued through Escuela Avancemos — a different school.🔶
5th Grade (Ashlie Spencer)Daily Substitute Permit issued through Chandler Park Academy — a different school.🔶
8th Grade Teacher (Volanda Frazier)Full-Year Basic Substitute permit only — no standard teaching certificate. Assigned as full-time Teacher of Record.⚠️
2 instructional staffProperly credentialed and correctly placed for their assignment.✅
2 staffExpired or pending credentials.⏳

Legend: ✅ Valid · ⚠️ Wrong endorsement/placement · ❌ No credentials · 🔶 Substitute permit from other school · ⏳ Expired

Source: MOECS public credential search, September 26, 2026. Staff titles from macdowellprep.com/about/.

The Rachel Webb Finding 📄 Documented

A kindergarten teacher holds a Secondary English/Journalism certification endorsed for grades 6–12.

Elementary education in Michigan requires a specific endorsement in early childhood or elementary education. A 6–12 secondary certification does not qualify an educator for K–5 instruction under Michigan law. MOECS shows Rachel Webb’s only endorsements are English 6–12 and Journalism 6–12 — neither covers kindergarten.

The Substitute Permit Problem 📄 Documented

Two MacDowell instructional staff hold Daily Substitute Permits issued through different schools:

StaffAssignmentPermit Issued Through
Alana Hubbell3rd GradeEscuela Avancemos — Detroit
Ashlie Spencer5th GradeChandler Park Academy — Harper Woods

Daily Substitute Permits are tied to the issuing school and are intended for temporary fill-in duty, not permanent full-time instructional positions. Using substitute permits from other schools to staff ongoing teaching roles is a credential compliance issue under Michigan law.

Volanda Frazier holds a Full-Year Basic Substitute permit as the full-time 8th grade Teacher of Record — a separate but related compliance problem.

The Law — MCL 388.1763 📄 Documented

Michigan Compiled Laws require charter school teachers to hold valid credentials:

“A teacher employed by or assigned to a public school academy shall hold a valid Michigan teaching certificate or a permit issued by the superintendent of public instruction.”

Penalty provisions when violations are found:

StatuteRequirement
MCL 388.1763(1)A district shall not employ an individual who is not appropriately placed under a valid certificate.
MCL 388.1763(2)50% state aid deduction for salary paid during the violation period.
MCL 388.1763(6)If a school official is notified by MDE and knowingly continues to employ an uncredentialed individual → misdemeanor, $1,500 fine per incident.

When MDE identifies credential violations, the statute requires enforcement — state aid deductions for uncredentialed employment and, where officials continue employment after notification, referral for criminal prosecution.

What MDE Did 📄 Documented

MDE was notified of credential problems at MacDowell. Over a four-year period, the Office of Educator Excellence investigated only one name — Brian Banks — in February 2022. The investigation was closed within approximately two hours after OEE Analyst Katie Schmiedeknecht communicated that “there will be no need for an investigation.”

MDE never checked the rest of the staff roster — despite MOECS and the Educator Registry (REP) being MDE’s own systems, searchable by any analyst in minutes.

Schmiedeknecht presents at state conferences on the same credential compliance rules she is charged with enforcing — including slides stating that “Any teacher who is not appropriately placed may be subject to a salary deduction based on MCL 388.1763.” Her office failed to enforce those rules at MacDowell while advising the school through the compliance loophole that avoided penalties for Banks.

Source: MDE FOIA response (September 25, 2026); MOECS public search (September 26, 2026).

Verify It Yourself

Anyone can reproduce this audit in minutes:

  1. Go to MOECS public search: mdoe.state.mi.us/MOECS/PublicCredentialSearch.aspx
  2. Enter the teacher’s last name
  3. Check: Is the certificate valid? Is it endorsed for the grades and subjects being taught?
  4. Compare results to the school’s actual staff roster at macdowellprep.com/about/

Discrepancies between MOECS endorsements and classroom assignments are visible immediately in the public record.

The Cost 📄 Documented

MacDowell Preparatory Academy serves 362 students. Four administrators draw $603,000/year in combined compensation:

MetricMacDowellContext
Admin cost per student$1,665/studentMichigan state average: approximately $850/student
Instructional spending32% of budgetMichigan target: 55–65%

Administration at nearly twice the state average per student diverts public funding away from instruction — in a school where MOECS already shows that most instructional staff lack proper credentials for their assignments.

This analysis is based entirely on MOECS public search results and Michigan Department of Education records. Every credential status can be independently verified using the steps above.

entry.title: Detroit Literacy Crisis — The Systemic View
entry.content:
MacDowell Preparatory Academy is not an anomaly — it is an extreme example of structural vulnerabilities in Michigan’s charter school oversight. This page connects the documented facts from this investigation to the broader patterns that enable them.

This analysis draws on the specific documented case to illustrate systemic patterns. The broader conclusions are the complainant’s analytical inference, supported by the specific evidence documented elsewhere on this site.

See also: Credential Audit, Funding Flow, Institutional Capture, Words vs. Numbers.

Five Structural Vulnerabilities

The MacDowell case documents five interlocking weaknesses in Michigan’s charter school accountability framework. The first four are structural mechanisms; the fifth is their cumulative effect on students.

1. Charter authorization as revenue 📄 Documented

Michigan authorizers receive 3% of state aid from each school they authorize. This creates a financial incentive to authorize and maintain schools regardless of performance.

At MacDowell Preparatory Academy, DPSCD (the authorizer) receives approximately $147K/year from that authorization fee alone — revenue that continues as long as the school remains open.

Source: MDE financial reports; charter authorization fee structure. See Funding Flow.

2. Management companies as extraction vehicles 📄 Documented

The Purpose Group LLC — Brian Banks’ management company — takes a 10% management fee plus all operating costs, totaling 72.67% of total revenue at MacDowell.

The fee-plus-cost-reimbursement structure means the management company can never lose money while the school absorbs all operational risk. Public per-pupil funding flows through the school entity; the majority exits to the LLC regardless of academic outcomes.

Source: MDE financial records; Purpose Group Management Agreement (FOIA). See Funding Flow and Purpose Group LLC.

3. Credential enforcement as theater 📄 Documented

The Michigan Department of Education investigated one name in four years at MacDowell — Brian Banks — in February 2022. The investigation was closed within approximately two hours after OEE Analyst Katie Schmiedeknecht communicated that “there will be no need for an investigation.”

MDE never checked the rest of the staff roster — despite MOECS and the Educator Registry being MDE’s own systems, searchable by any analyst in minutes. A MOECS audit on September 26, 2026 found that only 2 of 14 instructional staff are properly credentialed and correctly placed for their assignments.

Schmiedeknecht presents at state conferences on the same credential compliance rules her office is charged with enforcing — including slides stating that “Any teacher who is not appropriately placed may be subject to a salary deduction based on MCL 388.1763.” Her office failed to enforce those rules at MacDowell.

Source: MDE FOIA response (September 25, 2026); MOECS public search (September 26, 2026). See Credential Audit.

4. Board capture 📄 Documented

Judges, assistant attorneys general, and politicians sit on charter school boards, providing institutional legitimacy without corresponding accountability.

SchoolBoard ChairRole
MacDowell Preparatory AcademyJudge Tenisha Yancey36th District Court
Purpose Charter AcademyJudge Cylenthia MillerWayne County 3rd Circuit Court

These are not isolated appointments. The Institutional Capture analysis documents a broader pattern of judges, elected officials, and state employees serving on boards of schools connected to the Banks enterprise.

Source: School websites; Clutch Justice reporting (September 2026). See Tenisha Yancey, Cylenthia Miller.

5. Cumulative impact on students 📄 Documented

Every student at a bottom-3% school with 14% properly credentialed staff is a student who falls further behind. 362 students attend MacDowell Preparatory Academy.

MetricMacDowellSource
Math proficiency3%MDE, SchoolDigger
Statewide rankBottom 3% (1,443 of 1,488)SchoolDigger
Properly credentialed instructional staff2 of 14 (14%)MOECS audit, Sep 26, 2026
Enrollment362 studentsMDE records

The impact compounds annually. Students who enter kindergarten without credentialed teachers and leave middle school with 3% math proficiency carry deficits that accumulate across grade levels — not as a single-year failure, but as a structural outcome of the conditions documented above.

Source: MDE assessment data; SchoolDigger; Credential Audit.

The Numbers — General Context

The following points provide background context. They are cited as general patterns, not as specific statistics fabricated for this page.

  • Detroit’s overall literacy rates are among the lowest of any major American city.
  • Michigan has one of the highest proportions of charter school enrollment in the country.
  • Charter schools in Detroit have a wide performance range — some perform well, many do not.
  • The accountability mechanisms — authorizer oversight, MDE credential enforcement, financial auditing — have documented failure points at every level in this case. 📄 Documented

The specific numbers for MacDowell — 3% math proficiency, 72.67% revenue extraction, 14% properly credentialed staff — are documented on this site and in public records. The broader Detroit and Michigan context frames why a single school’s failure matters beyond its own walls.

What This Case Reveals 🔍 Inference

This is not just about Brian Banks. 🔍 Inference The structural vulnerabilities documented in this investigation exist across Michigan’s charter school sector:

  • Authorization incentives that prioritize revenue over oversight
  • Management company structures that extract more than they invest
  • Credential requirements that exist on paper but are not enforced
  • Governance structures that create conflicts of interest rather than accountability

Banks is the most extreme example documented in this investigation — 9 criminal convictions, fake credentials, 72.67% revenue extraction, 3% math proficiency. 📄 Documented But the structural enabling conditions are not unique to this case. 🔍 Inference

The same authorization fee model applies to every DPSCD-authorized charter. The same management company fee structure appears wherever a CMO operates under similar contract terms. The same MDE credential enforcement office serves every charter school in Michigan. The same board composition pattern — judges and public officials providing legitimacy — appears at multiple schools in this network.

MacDowell is the case study. The vulnerabilities are systemic. 🔍 Inference

Related Reporting

Independent journalism and public policy discussion provide broader context for the patterns documented here. This site does not reproduce those reports in full — it references them as external corroboration and context.

Clutch Justice

Clutch Justice has published reporting on Detroit charter school patterns connected to this investigation, including:

  • 📰 Clutch Justice : MacDowell: $15,217/student, 3% math proficiency — Academic and financial analysis of MacDowell’s extraction model, board composition, and DPSCD authorization chain
  • 📰 Clutch Justice : FOIA and Your Michigan School Board — Legal guide for parents requesting charter school records under Michigan FOIA

See the full Sources index for additional Clutch Justice references cited across this site.

National and State Policy Context

The broader national conversation about charter school accountability — including debates over authorizer incentives, management company transparency, and credential enforcement — provides policy context for the Michigan-specific patterns documented here. Michigan’s own charter school reform discussions address many of the same structural questions: who authorizes, who profits, and who enforces the rules when schools fail.

This site documents one case in detail. The policy conversation is larger than any single school.

Verify It Yourself

Every specific claim on this site can be independently checked against public records.

ResourceWhat to check
MiSchoolData.orgCompare charter school performance across Detroit — proficiency rates, enrollment, demographics
MI School DataSpending patterns by school — instruction vs. administration, management company payments
MOECS Public SearchTeacher credential verification — compare MOECS results to school staff rosters
This site’s evidence libraryDocumented case files — FOIA responses, financial records, management agreements
Verification pageStep-by-step instructions for reproducing every major claim

For the MacDowell credential audit specifically, see the reproduction steps in The Credential Gap.

The facts documented on this site are specific to the Banks enterprise. The structural analysis is the complainant’s inference, offered to support policy discussion and regulatory action. Every specific claim can be independently verified.

entry.title: Where the Money Goes — MacDowell Funding Flow Analysis
entry.content:
Lens: 🕸️ Topology ⚛️ Lattice 📅 Chronology 💰 Money ⚖️ Legal 🏛️ Capture

Michigan school funding follows a per-pupil model. State aid flows to the school based on enrollment. How schools allocate that funding determines what students actually receive. This analysis compares MacDowell Preparatory Academy’s spending patterns to state benchmarks and peer schools.

Spending Comparison

Instruction (teacher salaries, classroom)55-65%32.1%-23 to -33 points
Administration8-12%19.4%+7 to +11 points

The instruction line is 32.1% — well-run schools spend 55-65% on instruction. The missing 23-33 cents of every dollar is going to administration and the management company instead of the classroom.

Source: MDE financial reports, FY2025 audit data.

The Purpose Group Fee Structure

    B --> C["Purpose Group LLC<br/>72.67% of revenue"]

From the management agreement (OCR’d from FOIA):

Section 5.110% of Gross State School Aid ≈ $490K/year management fee

Section 5.2“No Related Parties” clause — violated on its face because Banks is sole member of Purpose Group AND superintendent of the school

The fee + cost reimbursement structure means Purpose Group can never lose money. The school absorbs all financial risk. Purpose Group absorbs all surplus.

What $4.9M Buys

Reading proficiency12%U.S. News
Statewide rankBottom 3% (1,443 of 1,488)SchoolDigger
Properly credentialed staff2 of 14 (14%)MOECS audit Sep 26, 2026

The Self-Dealing Structure

The management agreement creates a structural conflict of interest:

  1. Banks is sole member of Purpose Group LLC (the management company)
  2. Banks is superintendent of the school (hired by the management company)
  3. Banks controls the Purpose Foundation (the 501(c)(3))
  4. Purpose Group’s address is Banks’ home in Grosse Pointe Woods
  5. The management agreement’s “no related parties” clause is violated by the structure itself
flowchart TD
    A["Brian Banks"] --> B["controls Purpose Group LLC"]
    B --> C["manages MacDowell"]
    A --> D["is superintendent of MacDowell"]
    D --> E["hired by Purpose Group"]
    A --> F["controls Purpose Foundation"]
    F --> G["receives tax-deductible donations"]
    H["All three entities"] --> I["same controller, same beneficiary"]

The Authorization Incentive

DPSCD (Detroit Public Schools Community District) receives a 3% authorization fee from MacDowell’s state aid — approximately $147K/year. This creates a financial incentive to authorize and maintain charter schools, regardless of performance. DPSCD authorized PCA despite Banks’ 9 criminal convictions and MacDowell’s bottom-3% ranking.

Verify It Yourself

  • MiSchoolData.org — search MacDowell Preparatory Academy for financial data
  • Michigan LARA MiBusiness Registry — search “Purpose Group” for LLC registration
  • MDE Financial Reports — annual spending by category for any Michigan school

Every financial figure in this analysis is drawn from public records filed with the Michigan Department of Education and LARA. Clone the repository and verify independently.

Same system, other lenses:
  • 🕸️ Topology — Purpose Group LLC is the highest-degree entity node, connects to both schools, Banks, Holland, and all extraction edges
  • ⚛️ Lattice — The extraction percentage determines school quality, which determines capture effectiveness
  • 📅 Chronology — LLC formed before first charter, the extraction structure preceded the schools
  • ⚖️ Legal — Money laundering (18 USC 1956), predicate act 2 in the RICO pattern
  • 🏛️ Capture — Financial extraction is the revenue engine (Nexus 1) that funds all other nexus types

entry.title: The Land Deal — PCA's Building Purchase Option
entry.content:
The PCA charter contract with DPSCD includes a provision where Purpose Group LLC can purchase the school building at 10101 E. Canfield, Detroit. This provision is documented in the management agreement obtained via FOIA. This analysis examines the mechanism and its implications.

Source: Purpose Group Management Agreement (FOIA).

Analytical inference, not a legal finding. The implications described below reflect the complainant’s analysis of the contract mechanism and public records. They have not been adjudicated by any court or regulatory body.

The Mechanism

The building purchase option operates through a chain of charter authorization, management fees, and contractual property rights:

  1. DPSCD authorizes the charter. DPSCD authorizes Brian Banks to run Purpose Charter Academy in a district building at 10101 E. Canfield. Source: DPSCD charter authorization records; Purpose Group Management Agreement (FOIA).

  2. Purpose Group collects fees and costs. Banks’ management company, The Purpose Group LLC, collects 10% of state aid plus reimbursement for all operating costs under the management agreement. Source: Purpose Group Management Agreement (FOIA), Section 5.1 (10% of Gross State School Aid); Section 5.3 (operating cost reimbursement).

  3. Purpose Group can exercise the purchase option. After establishing the school, Purpose Group LLC can exercise a building purchase option embedded in the management agreement. Source: Purpose Group Management Agreement (FOIA), building purchase provision.

  4. Ownership transfers to the management company. If exercised, the building would be owned by Purpose Group LLC — the same entity that employs all staff and takes 72.67% of revenue from the sister school, MacDowell Preparatory Academy. Source: Purpose Group Management Agreement (FOIA); MDE financial records (72.67% revenue to Purpose Group LLC).

Who Benefits

PartyWhat They GetSource
Banks / Purpose GroupBuilding ownership (via purchase option) + 10% management fee + operating cost reimbursementPurpose Group Management Agreement (FOIA); MDE financial records
Judge Miller (PCA Board Chair)Board position at a publicly-funded school — governance powerPCA board records; DPSCD charter authorization
DPSCD3% authorization fee (~$147K/yr from MacDowell alone)MDE financial reports; charter authorization fee structure
Wells-Stallworth12+ year Board presidency at a $4.9M/yr operationMacDowell board records; MDE financial reports ($4.9M state aid)

Who Loses

PartyWhat They LoseSource
Students (362 MacDowell + PCA enrollment)Education outcomes — 3% math proficiency, 12% reading proficiency, uncredentialed teachersMDE assessment data; SchoolDigger; U.S. News; MOECS credential audit (Sep 26, 2026)
Michigan taxpayers$4.9M+/yr to an operation where 72.67% goes to one LLCMDE financial reports
Detroit public school systemPublic building potentially converted to private ownershipPurpose Group Management Agreement (FOIA), building purchase provision; DPSCD property records

The Pattern

This is not unique to Banks. Charter management organizations across the country have used similar building purchase provisions to convert public school property into private assets.

What makes this case distinctive — analytical inference — is the combination of factors present simultaneously:

  • A building purchase option exists in the PCA management agreement
  • The management company is controlled by a superintendent with 9 criminal convictions
  • The sister school (MacDowell) is ranked in the bottom 3% of Michigan (1,443 of 1,488)

Sources: Purpose Group Management Agreement (FOIA); DPSCD authorization records; SchoolDigger statewide ranking; criminal conviction records on file.

Verify It Yourself

  • Wayne County Register of Deeds — search 10101 E. Canfield for property records
  • DPSCD Charter Authorization records — public meeting minutes and authorization documents
  • Michigan LARA MiBusiness Registry — search “Purpose Group” for LLC registration

This analysis is based on the Purpose Group Management Agreement obtained via FOIA and public property records. The contract language is available in the evidence repository.
